BuCQ4.question: In general, the ridership of the metro system increases as the number of stations increases. True or False?
BuCQ4.reference_chain: MAP(size(bubble) → ridership | legend) → MAP(x → stations) → SCAN({bubble[*]} along xaxis) → CORR(x, size(bubble)) ≈ 0 (e.g. OUTLIER: bubble[Beijing] high-x small; bubble[Tokyo] low-x largest) → ANSWER(False)
BuCQ4.notes: This item requires relating a position channel (x = stations) to a size channel (ridership). The successful path was usually a counterexample: Beijing (far right, tiny) and Tokyo (left, largest) are the pivotal bubbles, often marked by dropping vertical lines from the bubbles to the x-axis. A smaller group scanned along x and reported no pattern. Errors came from prior-knowledge reasoning, perceiving an upward trend while dismissing exceptions, tracing a position trendline (length against stations) instead of using size, or deciding that no relation meant the question was unanswerable. Two participants reasoned correctly but said they mis-clicked True.

new_symbols.trendline: (spec) used for a line the participant draws through bubble positions
new_symbols.region[quadrants]: a partition of the plot into regions by drawn cross-hair lines

strategies.chain: FIND(counterexample: bubble high-x & small, e.g. Beijing / bubble low-x & large, e.g. Tokyo) → PROJ(→ xaxis) → CMP(size vs x) → CORR≠+ → ANSWER(False)
strategies.quote: Beijing has a small bubble and is far to the right, whereas Tokyo is closer to the left (low number of stations) yet has a large bubble

BuCQ5.question: The average metro system in this chart has approximately 300 stations 200km in length
BuCQ5.reference_chain: SCAN({bubble[*]}) → READ(x) per bubble (≈200…740) → AVG(x)≈440 → READ(y) per bubble → AVG(y)≈310 → CMP((440,310) vs (300,200)) → ANSWER(False)  [shortcut: COUNT({bubble: x>300 ∧ y>200}) = most, so the mean is above both targets]
BuCQ5.notes: This item asks for the mean of 11 points, and the chart shows no average, so a quarter of participants said it was impossible or unclear. The most common sketch is a cross-hair to the target point (300 stations, 200 km). From there people split: those who noticed the bubbles sit mostly above and to the right of it said False, while those who looked for a bubble at exactly that point and found none answered Not sure or Impossible. Correct reasoners counted bubbles beyond the thresholds or estimated and averaged x-values (one wrote out 4440/11 = 444). Wrong True answers came from substitutes for the mean: majority counts, a diagonal centre line, the midrange of extremes, or a single bubble near the target (Tokyo).

BuCQ6.question: Which city's metro system has the largest number of stations?
BuCQ6.reference_chain: MAP(x → stations | xtitle) → SCAN({bubble[*]} along xaxis) → ARGMAX({bubble[*]}, x)=bubble[Shanghai] (≈740, just right of Beijing ≈725) → ANSWER(Shanghai)
BuCQ6.notes: All 7 trials in this group are wrong, and 6 answered Tokyo: they took the largest bubble (the size channel, ridership) rather than the rightmost one (x = stations). Two participants caught this afterwards and circled Shanghai, explicitly naming the size-versus-numbers confusion. One used the wrong position axis (N.Y.C is highest on y = length). The pivotal elements are the x-axis title and the close pair Shanghai/Beijing at the right edge, which no wrong answer attended to. With only 7 trials, all incorrect, this sample shows error strategies and says nothing about how often the item is answered correctly.
